**UNICEF** ([/ˈ j uː n i ˌ s ɛ f/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_YOO-nee-SEF_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")), originally the **United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund**, officially **United Nations Children's Fund** since 1953,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-4) is an agency of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") responsible for providing [humanitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarianism "Humanitarianism") and [developmental aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_aid "Development aid") to [children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child "Child") worldwide.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-6) The organization is one of the most widely known and visible social welfare entities globally, operating in 192 countries and territories.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-7) UNICEF's activities include providing immunizations and disease prevention, administering [treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiretroviral_drug "Antiretroviral drug") for children and mothers with [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV"), enhancing childhood and [maternal nutrition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maternal_nutrition "Maternal nutrition"), improving [sanitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation "Sanitation"), promoting education, and providing [emergency relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_relief "Emergency relief") in response to disasters.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-8)

UNICEF is the successor of the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund, and was created on 11 December 1946, in New York, by the [United Nations Relief Rehabilitation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Relief_and_Rehabilitation_Administration "United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration") to provide immediate relief to children and mothers affected by [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). The same year, the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") established UNICEF to further institutionalize post-war relief work.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-9) In 1950, its mandate was extended to address the long-term needs of children and women, particularly in [developing countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_country "Developing country"). In 1953, the organization became a permanent part of the [United Nations System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_System "United Nations System"), and its name was changed to United Nations Children's Fund, though it retains the UNICEF acronym.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-FAQ-2)

UNICEF relies entirely on voluntary contributions from governments and private donors. Its total income as of 2024 was $8.61 billion, of which public-sector partners contributed $4.92 billion.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-10) It is governed by a 36-member executive board that establishes policies, approves programs, and oversees administrative and financial plans. The board is made up of government representatives elected by the [United Nations Economic and Social Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Economic_and_Social_Council "United Nations Economic and Social Council"), usually for three-year terms.

UNICEF's programs emphasize developing community-level services to promote the health and well-being of children. Most of its work is in the field, with a network that includes 150 country offices, headquarters and other facilities, and 34 "national committees" that carry out its mission through programs developed with host governments. Seven regional offices provide technical assistance to country offices as needed, while its Supply Division—based in the cities of [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen") and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")—helps provide over $3 billion in critical aid and services.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-SD-11)

In 2018, UNICEF assisted in the birth of 27 million babies, administered [pentavalent vaccines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DTwP-HepB-Hib_vaccine "DTwP-HepB-Hib vaccine") to an estimated 65.5 million children, provided education for 12 million children, treated four million children with [severe acute malnutrition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_acute_malnutrition "Severe acute malnutrition"), and responded to 285 humanitarian emergencies in 90 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-12) UNICEF has received recognition for its work, including the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") in [1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Nobel_Peace_Prize "1965 Nobel Peace Prize"), the [Indira Gandhi Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi_Prize "Indira Gandhi Prize") in 1989 and the [Princess of Asturias Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Asturias_Awards "Prince of Asturias Awards") in 2006. During the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, UNICEF, along with the [World Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization") and other agencies, published guidance about healthy parenting.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-13)

## History of formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of formation")]

### Creation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Creation")]

As early as September 1943, Polish health specialist [Ludwik Rajchman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwik_Rajchman "Ludwik Rajchman") suggested in an article published in _[Free World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free\_World\_(magazine) "Free World (magazine)")_ entitled "A United Nations Health Service—Why not?" that a health service should be incorporated into the future international organization. He also proposed a "health tax" paid by member states.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-bma-14)

At the 1948 dissolution of the [United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Relief_and_Rehabilitation_Administration "United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration") (UNRRA), Rajchman proposed to use its residual funds for a child-feeding program beneficiary of US funding.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-MJ-15) The organization was created by resolution 57(I) of the United Nations General Assembly on 11 December 1946 and named United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF). As its first chairman, Rajchman chose [Maurice Pate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Pate "Maurice Pate") of the [Commission for Relief in Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_for_Relief_in_Belgium "Commission for Relief in Belgium") to direct the agency and "to think about organizing an action, a fund for the benefit of children, war victims chiefly."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-MJ-15) Rajchman, as head of a special UN subcommittee and with the support of [La Guardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiorello_La_Guardia "Fiorello La Guardia"), [Herbert Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover "Herbert Hoover") and Maurice Pate, presented the resolution to the [General assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_assembly "General assembly").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-bma-14) From a temporary emergency relief agency in 1946 providing food and clothing to children and mothers displaced by [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the agency became a permanent UN Organization in 1953,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-MJ-15) and extended its efforts toward general programs of children welfare.

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Governance")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Sudan_Envoy_-_UNICEF_Tent.jpg/250px-Sudan_Envoy_-_UNICEF_Tent.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sudan_Envoy_-_UNICEF_Tent.jpg)

UNICEF-care tent in [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan")

UNICEF relies on country offices to help carry out its work through a unique program of cooperation developed with the host government. The program seeks to develop practical strategies for fulfilling and [protecting the rights of children and women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarian_protection "Humanitarian protection"). Regional offices guide this work and provide technical assistance to country offices as needed. Overall management and administration of the organization take place at its headquarters in New York City.

Guiding and monitoring all of UNICEF's work is an executive board made up of 36 members who are government representatives. The board establishes policies, approves programs, and decides on administrative and financial plans and budgets. Its work is coordinated by the bureau, comprising the president and four vice-presidents, each officer representing one of the five regional groups. These five officers are elected by the executive board annually from among its members, with the presidency rotating among the regional groups on an annual basis. As a matter of custom, permanent members of the Security Council do not serve as officers of the executive board.

The office of the secretary of the executive board helps maintain an effective relationship between the executive board and the UNICEF secretariat, and organizes field visits by board members.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-18)

## UNICEF national committees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: UNICEF national committees")]

See also: [List of UNICEF national committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UNICEF_national_committees "List of UNICEF national committees")

There are national committees in 34 countries, each established as an independent local [non-governmental organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization "Non-governmental organization"). Their primary function is to raise funds from the private sector, as UNICEF is entirely dependent on voluntary contributions.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-20) National committees collectively account for about one-third of the agency's annual income, including from corporations, civil society organizations, around six million individual donors worldwide.

## Promotion and fundraising

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Promotion and fundraising")]

In the United States, [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") and some other countries, UNICEF is known for its "[Trick-Or-Treat for UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trick-or-Treat_for_UNICEF "Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF")" program in which children collect money for UNICEF from the houses they [trick-or-treat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trick-or-treating "Trick-or-treating") on [Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween "Halloween") night, sometimes instead of candy. The program was discontinued in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") in 2006.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-21)

UNICEF is present in 191 countries and territories around the world, but not involved in nine others ([Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas"), [Brunei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunei "Brunei"), [Cyprus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus "Cyprus"), [Latvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvia "Latvia"), [Liechtenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liechtenstein "Liechtenstein"), [Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malta "Malta"), [Mauritius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritius "Mauritius"), [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco"), [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), and [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan")).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-22)

Many people in [developed countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_countries "Developed countries") first hear about UNICEF's work through the activities of one of the 36 [national committees for UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UNICEF_national_committees "List of UNICEF national committees"). These [non-governmental organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organizations "Non-governmental organizations") (NGOs) are primarily responsible for [fundraising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundraising "Fundraising"), selling UNICEF greeting cards and products, creating private and public partnerships, advocating for children's rights, and providing other support. The US Fund for UNICEF is the oldest of the national committees, founded in 1946.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-23)

On 19 April 2007, [Grand Duchess Maria Teresa of Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchess_Maria_Teresa_of_Luxembourg "Grand Duchess Maria Teresa of Luxembourg") was appointed UNICEF Eminent Advocate for Children,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-24) in which role she has visited Brazil (2007),[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-25) China (2008),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-26) and Burundi (2009).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-27)

In 2009, the British retailer [Tesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesco "Tesco") used "Change for Good" as advertising, which is trademarked by UNICEF for charity usage but not for commercial or retail use. This prompted the agency to say, "it is the first time in Unicef's history that a commercial entity has purposely set out to capitalize on one of our campaigns and subsequently damage an income stream which several of our programs for children are dependent on". They went on to call on the public "who have children's welfare at heart, to consider carefully who they support when making consumer choices".[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-29) "Change for Good" is also supported by Australian airline [Qantas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qantas "Qantas"), relying on passengers to fundraise via a given envelope since 1991, and has raised over $36 million, with over 19,500 kg of coins every year.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-30)[Frequent flyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequent-flyer_program "Frequent-flyer program") can also redeem their mile points to donate.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-31) Norman Gillespie, UNICEF Australia's chief executive, said "If every Qantas passenger traveling domestically gave us just a few of their forgotten coins each time they traveled it would make little difference to their day, but a world of difference in saving children's lives." This mode of support has to change with time in to a digital forum according to Gerard Devan UNICEF’s Head of Development.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-32)

### Aid transparency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Aid transparency")]

UNICEF regularly publishes to the [International Aid Transparency Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Aid_Transparency_Initiative "International Aid Transparency Initiative") (IATI) using the identifier XM-DAC-41122.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-33) The organisation has been included assessed on its transparency by [Publish What You Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publish_What_You_Fund "Publish What You Fund") since 2012 and is included in the 2024 Aid Transparency Index[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-34) with an overall score of 86.2 which is categorised as a "very good" score.

## Sponsorship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Sponsorship")]

In 2003, UNICEF sponsored Italian football club [Piacenza Calcio 1919](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piacenza_Calcio_1919 "Piacenza Calcio 1919") until 2008.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Messi_ball_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Messi_ball_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Messi_ball_(cropped).jpg)

Lionel Messi sporting the FC Barcelona Jersey with UNICEF sponsorship

In 2005, an advertisement featuring [The Smurfs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Smurfs "The Smurfs") was aired in Belgium in which the Smurf village is annihilated by warplanes. Designed as a UNICEF advertisement, and with the approval of the family of the Smurfs' late creator [Peyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peyo "Peyo"), the 25-second episode was shown on the national television after the 9 p.m. timeslot to avoid children having to see it. It was the keystone in a fund-raising campaign by UNICEF's Belgian arm to raise money for the rehabilitation of former child soldiers in Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo—both former Belgian colonies.

On 7 September 2006, an agreement between UNICEF and the Spanish Catalan [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club [FC Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona") was reached whereby the club would donate €1.5 million per year to the organization for five years. As part of the agreement, FC Barcelona would wear the UNICEF logo on the front of their uniforms in yellow (as seen in the picture on the right of Lionel Messi).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-35) This was the first time a football club sponsored an organization rather than the other way around. It was also the first time in FC Barcelona's history that they have had another organization's name across the front of their uniform. In 2016, the team signed a new four-year sponsorship deal with UNICEF guaranteeing the organization £1.58 million per year and free advertising. From 2022 onwards, Barcelona has made a partnership with Swedish company [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") and has since put the [UNHCR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Refugee_Agency "United Nations Refugee Agency") logo in gold at the bottom of the back of their jerseys.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-36)

In January 2007, UNICEF struck a partnership with Canada's national [tent pegging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tent_pegging "Tent pegging") team. The team was officially re-flagged as "UNICEF Team Canada", and its riders wear UNICEF's logo in competition, and team members promote and raise funds for UNICEF's campaign against childhood HIV-AIDS.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-37)

The Swedish club [Hammarby IF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammarby_Fotboll "Hammarby Fotboll") followed the Spanish and Canadian lead on 14 April 2007,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-38) also raising funds for UNICEF and displaying the UNICEF name on their sportswear. The Danish football club [Brøndby IF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%B8ndby_IF "Brøndby IF") participated in a similar arrangement from 2008 to 2013.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-39)

In 2007, NASCAR driver [Jacques Villeneuve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Villeneuve "Jacques Villeneuve") has occasionally placed the UNICEF logo on the #27 [Bill Davis Racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Davis_Racing "Bill Davis Racing") pickup truck in the [NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASCAR_Craftsman_Truck_Series "NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-40)

In honour of their 50th anniversary in 2008, the Smurfs began a year-long "Happy Smurfday Euro Tour" in connection with UNICEF. The Smurfs visited fifteen European countries on the day of their 50th "Smurfday" in the form of publicly distributed white figurines. The recipients could decorate and submit them to a competition. The results of this contest were auctioned off and raised a total amount of 124,700 euros for benefit of UNICEF.

Australian [A-League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-League "A-League") club [Sydney FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_FC "Sydney FC") announced they would also enter into a partnership with UNICEF raising funds for children in the [Asia-Pacific region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia-Pacific "Asia-Pacific"), and would also display the UNICEF logo for the remainder of the [2011-12 A-League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011-12_A-League "2011-12 A-League") season.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-41)

In [Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana "Botswana"), UNICEF has funded the development of new state-of-the-art HIV/AIDS education for every schoolchild in Botswana from nonprofit organization [TeachAids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TeachAids "TeachAids").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-42)

UNICEF announced a landmark partnership with [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") club [Rangers F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangers_F.C. "Rangers F.C.") UNICEF partnered with the Rangers Charity Foundation and pledged to raise £300,000 by 2011.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-43)

In 2010, UNICEF created a partnership with [Phi Iota Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Iota_Alpha "Phi Iota Alpha"), making them the first Greek Lettered Organization UNICEF has ever worked with. In 2011, Phi Iota Alpha raised over $20,000 for the Tap Project and the Trick or Treats for UNICEF Campaign.

In 2013, they agreed a contract with Greek association football champions [Olympiacos F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiacos_F.C. "Olympiacos F.C.") who will show the organization's logo on the front of their shirts.

### UNICEF Kid Power

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: UNICEF Kid Power")]

Main article: [UNICEF Kid Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF_Kid_Power "UNICEF Kid Power")

Started in 2015, Kid Power is a division of UNICEF that was created as an effort to involve kids in helping other kids in need. UNICEF Kid Power developed the world's first **"Wearable for Good"**,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-44) called Kid Power Bands,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-45) which is a kids' fitness tracker bracelet that connects to a smartphone app. The app lets users complete missions, which counts total steps and awards points. The points then unlock funding from partners, which is then used by UNICEF to deliver lifesaving packets of therapeutic food to severely malnourished children around the world.

### Trick-or-Treat UNICEF box

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Trick-or-Treat UNICEF box")]

Main article: [Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trick-or-Treat_for_UNICEF "Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF")

Since 1950, when a group of children in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), donated $17 which they received on Halloween to help post-World War II victims, the Trick-or-Treat UNICEF box has become a tradition in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") during the fall.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-46) These small orange boxes are handed to children at schools and other locations before 31 October. UNICEF works directly with companies to improve their business practices, bringing them in line with obligations under [international law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_law "International law"), and ensuring that they respect children's rights in the realms of the marketplace, workplace, and the community. ### Girl Star

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Girl Star")]

The [Girl Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girl_Star?action=edit&redlink=1 "Girl Star (page does not exist)")[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-53) project is a series of films which documents stories of girls from the most disadvantaged communities across five northern states in India who, through education, have managed to break socio-economic constraints to make a success of their lives and become self-sufficient. ### U-report

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: U-report")]

[U-Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-Report "U-Report") is a free SMS social monitoring tool and real-time information system for community participation, designed to strengthen community-led development, citizen engagement, and positive change. SMS polls and alerts are sent out to U-reporters and real-time response information is collected. Results and ideas are shared back with the community. Issues polled include among others health, education, water, sanitation and hygiene, youth unemployment, HIV/ AIDS, disease outbreaks; social welfare sectors. The initiative is currently operational in 68 countries and covers more than 11 million people.

### UNICEF Innocenti Research Centre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: UNICEF Innocenti Research Centre")]

The UNICEF [Innocenti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ospedale_degli_Innocenti "Ospedale degli Innocenti") Research Centre was established in 1988. It is based at the Ospedale degli Innocenti historic building in [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-unicefinnocentihistory-60)

The centre was created to strengthen UNICEF's research capability and to support its advocacy for children worldwide. It is the research arm of UNICEF, and is part of the Office of Research. The Office of Research has as its prime objectives to improve international understanding of issues relating to children's rights, to promote economic policies that advance the cause of children, and to help facilitate the full implementation of the United Nations [Convention on the Rights of the Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_on_the_Rights_of_the_Child "Convention on the Rights of the Child") in 190 countries and territories.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-61)

UNICEF Innocenti develops its research agenda in consultation with other parts of UNICEF and with external stakeholders.

The program reaffirms the centre's academic freedom and the focus of IRC's research on knowledge gaps, emerging questions and sensitive issues which are relevant to the realization of children's rights, in developing and industrialized countries. It capitalizes on IRC's role as an interface between UNICEF field experience, international experts, research networks and policy makers and is designed to strengthen the centre's institutional collaboration with regional academic and policy institutions, pursuing the following goals:

*   Generation and communication of strategic and influential knowledge on issues affecting children and the realization of their rights;
*   Knowledge exchange and brokering;
*   Support to UNICEF's advocacy, policy's and program development in support of the Millennium Agenda;
*   Securing and strengthening the centre's institutional and financial basis.

Three interrelated strategies guide the achievement of these goals:

*   Evidence-based analysis drawing on quantitative and qualitative information, the application of appropriate methodologies, and the development of recommendations to assess and inform advocacy and policy action.
*   Enhanced partnerships with research and policy institutions and development actors, globally and at regional level, in developing and industrialized countries.
*   Communication and leveraging of research findings and recommendations to support policy development and advocacy initiatives through strategic dissemination of studies and contribution to relevant events and fora.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-62)

## Position on ethical themes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Position on ethical themes")]

UNICEF's programmatic objectives include the promotion of safe [abortions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion")[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-63) and education in [family planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_population_planning "Human population planning") and in the use of [contraception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraception "Contraception").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-65) To this end, it is one of the co-sponsors of the [Special Programme on Human Reproduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Programme_on_Human_Reproduction "Special Programme on Human Reproduction").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-SRH-66)

In a joint declaration of 2011,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-67) UNICEF argued the need to combat the spread of selective abortion, through plans that favored, inter alia, the use of safe abortion services and family planning programs in order to decrease the use of abortion.

In 2013, together with WHO, it published an integrated plan of guidelines for the prevention of infant mortality caused by pneumonia and diarrhea, including, among the recommended strategies for promoting the health of women and children, access to safe abortion.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-68)

UNICEF has adopted the ABC strategy ("**a**bstinence, **b**e faithful and consistent **c**ondom use") promoted in various international AIDS prevention interventions.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-69) The strategy was later updated as the "**ABC to Z** model", to include **D**elaying and **V**oluntary **C**ounselling &**T**esting.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-70)

In 1996, the [Vatican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_See "Holy See") withdrew its symbolic contribution to UNICEF on the occasion of the publication by UNICEF of a manual on emergency operations for refugee populations which supported the spread of [emergency contraceptive practices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_contraception "Emergency contraception").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-71)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-72)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-73)

Despite this, on several occasions, senior UNICEF officials have denied that the organization promoted abortion or family planning methods.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-75)

UNICEF also supports the adoption by states of laws that guarantee [LGBT couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexual_union "Homosexual union") and their children the legal recognition of their status, as these rules would help ensure the best interests of children.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-76)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Controversies")]

### Adoption program

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Adoption program")]

UNICEF has a policy preferring orphanages only be used as temporary accommodation for children when there is no alternative. UNICEF has historically opposed the creation of large-scale, permanent orphanages for children, preferring instead to find children places in their (extended) families and communities, wherever possible. This has led UNICEF to be skeptical of international adoption efforts as a solution to child care problems in developing countries; UNICEF has preferred to see children cared for in their birth countries rather than be adopted by foreign parents.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-78)

A 2013 article in _[U.S. News & World Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.\_News\_&\_World\_Report "U.S. News & World Report")_ magazine reported that UNICEF conditions large cash payments to developing countries upon the adoption of UNICEF's recommendations for the welfare of orphaned children, and asserted that "[t]oo often, UNICEF’s intervention leads to a cessation of international adoptions until all of its recommendations are in place".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-79)

### Child mortality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Child mortality")]

One concern is that the child [mortality rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") has not decreased in some areas as rapidly as had been planned, especially in Sub-Saharan Africa, where in 2013 "the region still has the highest child mortality rate: 92 deaths per 1000 live births",[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-CMEp1-80) and that "Globally, nearly half of under-five deaths are attributable to undernutrition."

In 2005, [Richard Horton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Horton_(editor) "Richard Horton (editor)"), editor-in-chief of _[The Lancet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lancet "The Lancet")_, editorialized that "over 60% of these deaths were and remain preventable" and that the coverage levels for these interventions are "appallingly low in the 42 countries that account for 90% of child deaths".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-horton-81)

A $27 million UNICEF program in [West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa") in 2001–2005 which was meant to decrease child deaths from disease has been deemed a failure, according to a study that found higher survival rates of children in some regions that were not included in that program.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-82)

Wendy McElroy has argued that UNICEF's focus on rights rather than safety and survival is idealistic, and that by focusing on politicized [children's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_rights "Children's rights") instead of mere child survival, UNICEF has contributed indirectly to the [child mortality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_mortality "Child mortality") crisis.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-83)

### Mismanagement and abuse of funding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Mismanagement and abuse of funding")]

In 1995, in what was called "the worst scandal in its history", UNICEF disclosed that 24 employees in its Kenya office stole or squandered $10-million; this fraud consumed more than a quarter of the UNICEF's $37-million two-year budget for Kenya.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-84)

In Germany, in the late 2000s, UNICEF was accused of mismanagement, abuse and waste of funds.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-85) This has resulted in 5,000 of UNICEF regular donors abandoning their support from the charity, and politicians and public figures, including [Angela Merkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Merkel "Angela Merkel"), demanding explanations, and the chairwoman of UNICEF Germany resigning in 2008.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-86)

In 2012, UNICEF confirmed fraud in a Pakistan school rehabilitation project, where an estimated US$4 million was lost when funds were misappropriated.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-87)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-88)

### NSA surveillance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: NSA surveillance")]

Further information: [Global surveillance disclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_surveillance_disclosure "Global surveillance disclosure")

Documents released by [Edward Snowden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden "Edward Snowden") in December 2013 showed that UNICEF was among the surveillance targets of British and American intelligence agencies.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-89)

### Sexual assault

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Sexual assault")]

Press reports in 2020 disclosed that women in the [Democratic Republic of Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_Congo "Democratic Republic of Congo") accused foreign aid workers, including UNICEF workers, of sexually assaulting them. [The World Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization") described the alleged actions as reprehensible and a UNICEF spokesperson acknowledged that such sexual assault cases are underreported in the region.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-90) Prior to this, in 2018, UNICEF was hit by a wave of sexual misconduct accusations; in 2018, deputy director [Justin Forsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Forsyth "Justin Forsyth") resigned from UNICEF following allegations that he behaved inappropriately toward female staff members.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-91)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-92)

### Child sexual abuse

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Child sexual abuse")]

In 1988, Jozef Verbeeck, director of UNICEF's Belgium committee, was convicted for offences relating to his knowledge of an international [child sex ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_sex_ring "Child sex ring") operating out of a UNICEF office in Brussels. The group was coordinated by Michel Felu, a UNICEF employee who installed a photo lab in the cellar of the office to develop pictures of children engaged in obscene acts.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-93) Over a thousand photographs were seized by Belgian police, along with a mailing list of over 400 names in 15 European countries that originated on a UNICEF computer.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-94)

UNICEF has also admitted to shortcomings in its humanitarian support of children who said that they were raped and sexually abused by French peacekeepers in [Central African Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Republic "Central African Republic").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-95)

Peter Newell, a convicted child sex offender, has worked closely with UNICEF: he managed a charity that received hundreds of thousand of pounds from the NSPCC, Barnardo's, Save the Children and UNICEF; and cowrote a manual on children's rights called _Implementation Handbook for the Convention on the Rights of the Child for Unicef_, which was published by UNICEF.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-97)

Andrew MacLeod, the former chief of operations at the UN's Emergency Co-ordination Center, had accused UNICEF of failure to take action to prevent abuses; he stated "There are tens of thousands of aid workers around the world with [pedophile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedophile "Pedophile") tendencies, but if you wear a UNICEF T-shirt, nobody will ask what you're up to."[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-99)

### Funding of UK food charities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Funding of UK food charities")]

In December 2020, UNICEF made funding available to feed children in the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") for the first time as part of its Food Power for Generation COVID initiative. UNICEF pledged £25,000 to School Food Matters, a south London charity, to help feed children over the Christmas holidays. A partnership of Devon charities had also been given £24,000 to help feed 120 families over the winter of 2020. UNICEF said it was helping children in the UK because of an increase in food poverty in Britain, caused by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"). It estimates there are children going hungry in a fifth of households. Anna Kettley, from UNICEF said "We are one of the richest countries in the world and we should not have to be relying on food banks or food aid." [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") MP [Zarah Sultana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarah_Sultana "Zarah Sultana") in the House of Commons said, "For the first time ever, UNICEF, the UN agency responsible for providing humanitarian aid to children, is having to feed working-class kids in the UK but while children go hungry, a wealthy few enjoy obscene riches." In response, [Jacob Rees-Mogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Rees-Mogg "Jacob Rees-Mogg"), [Tory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tory "Tory") MP and [Leader of the House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_House_of_Commons "Leader of the House of Commons") said, "I think it is a real scandal that UNICEF should be playing politics in this way when it is meant to be looking after people in the poorest, the most deprived, countries of the world where people are starving, where there are famines and where there are civil wars, and they make cheap political points of this kind, giving, I think, 25,000 to one council. It is a political stunt of the lowest order. UNICEF should be ashamed of itself." Chris Forster, from Transforming Plymouth Together, one of the Devon charities to benefit from UNICEF donations, said, "We had one family as part of the deliveries last week literally in tears with gratitude because their cupboard was bare." [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") MP, [Tommy Sheppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Sheppard_(politician) "Tommy Sheppard (politician)") said, "It is astonishing that these comments are coming from the same government that had to be publicly shamed into following Scotland's lead and providing free school meals for children over the holidays." [LBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LBC "LBC") reported that the UN humanitarian aid agency are providing over £700,000 to feed hungry children in the UK.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-100)

### "Digital Age Assurance Tools and Children's Rights Online across the Globe" report

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=UNICEF&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: \"Digital Age Assurance Tools and Children's Rights Online across the Globe\" report")]

In 2021, UNICEF published a report called "Digital Age Assurance Tools and Children's Rights Online across the Globe".[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-Snopes-101) The paper, focusing on human rights and digital tools, generated controversy after misleading claims and headlines about the report were spread online, originating from a story by the conservative [Center for Family and Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Family_and_Human_Rights "Center for Family and Human Rights").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-Snopes-101) The fact-checking website [Snopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snopes "Snopes") rated the claim that the "report said pornography is not always harmful to children and blocking children from watching pornography online violates their rights" as false.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-Snopes-101) UNICEF pulled down the report, citing misrepresentation of one of its portions.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF#cite_note-Snopes-101)

_**Hi Bye, Mama!**_ ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"):하이바이, 마마!) is a 2020 [South Korean television series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_drama "Korean drama") starring Kim Tae-hee, [Lee Kyu-hyung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyu-hyung "Lee Kyu-hyung"), and [Go Bo-gyeol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_Bo-gyeol "Go Bo-gyeol"). It aired on [tvN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVN_(South_Korean_TV_channel) "TVN (South Korean TV channel)") from February 22 to April 19, 2020.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-2)

## Synopsis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hi_Bye,_Mama!&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Synopsis")]

Cha Yu-ri (Kim Tae-hee) has been a ghost since she died in a tragic accident five years ago. Through a [reincarnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebirth_(Buddhism) "Rebirth (Buddhism)") project, she is given the possibility to become human again if she succeeds in going back to her place within 49 days. However, her husband, Cho Gang-hwa ([Lee Kyu-hyung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyu-hyung "Lee Kyu-hyung")), is now remarried. She has to choose between her own or her husband's happiness.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-3)

## Cast

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hi_Bye,_Mama!&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cast")]

### Main

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hi_Bye,_Mama!&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Main")]

*   Kim Tae-hee as Cha Yu-ri[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-5)

She becomes a lingering ghost after getting hit by a car while 9 months pregnant. After being taken to the hospital where her husband works, her daughter is saved, however Yu-ri is unable to survive. Four years later, Yu-ri becomes human again after having an emotional outburst towards God for the tragedy that befell her, and is granted 49 days to regain her place as Gang-hwa's wife and her daughter's mother in order to be able to stay permanently. If she is unable to do so, she must willfully go to heaven and reincarnate.
*   [Lee Kyu-hyung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyu-hyung "Lee Kyu-hyung") as Cho Gang-hwa[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-6)

A well off doctor and former surgeon. After his wife's death, he begins to distance himself from reality, becoming depressed. He develops a trauma of surgery after losing his pregnant wife because he was unreachable and locked up in an operating room.
*   [Go Bo-gyeol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_Bo-gyeol "Go Bo-gyeol") as Oh Min-jung

Gang-hwa's new wife, who later discovers Gang-hwa's true feelings and about Yu-ri's resurrection. Current mother figure of Yu-ri's daughter Seo-woo.

_**Hi Bye, Mama!**_ ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"):하이바이, 마마!) is a 2020 [South Korean television series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_drama "Korean drama") starring Kim Tae-hee, [Lee Kyu-hyung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyu-hyung "Lee Kyu-hyung"), and [Go Bo-gyeol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_Bo-gyeol "Go Bo-gyeol"). It aired on [tvN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVN_(South_Korean_TV_channel) "TVN (South Korean TV channel)") from February 22 to April 19, 2020.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-2)

## Synopsis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hi_Bye,_Mama!&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Synopsis")]

Cha Yu-ri (Kim Tae-hee) has been a ghost since she died in a tragic accident five years ago. Through a [reincarnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebirth_(Buddhism) "Rebirth (Buddhism)") project, she is given the possibility to become human again if she succeeds in going back to her place within 49 days. However, her husband, Cho Gang-hwa ([Lee Kyu-hyung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyu-hyung "Lee Kyu-hyung")), is now remarried. She has to choose between her own or her husband's happiness.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-3)

## Cast

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hi_Bye,_Mama!&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cast")]

### Main

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hi_Bye,_Mama!&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Main")]

*   Kim Tae-hee as Cha Yu-ri[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-5)

She becomes a lingering ghost after getting hit by a car while 9 months pregnant. After being taken to the hospital where her husband works, her daughter is saved, however Yu-ri is unable to survive. Four years later, Yu-ri becomes human again after having an emotional outburst towards God for the tragedy that befell her, and is granted 49 days to regain her place as Gang-hwa's wife and her daughter's mother in order to be able to stay permanently. If she is unable to do so, she must willfully go to heaven and reincarnate.
*   [Lee Kyu-hyung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyu-hyung "Lee Kyu-hyung") as Cho Gang-hwa[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi_Bye,_Mama!#cite_note-6)

A well off doctor and former surgeon. After his wife's death, he begins to distance himself from reality, becoming depressed. He develops a trauma of surgery after losing his pregnant wife because he was unreachable and locked up in an operating room.
*   [Go Bo-gyeol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_Bo-gyeol "Go Bo-gyeol") as Oh Min-jung

Gang-hwa's new wife, who later discovers Gang-hwa's true feelings and about Yu-ri's resurrection. Current mother figure of Yu-ri's daughter Seo-woo.
